title: This Death Valley Plant Stays Cool by 'Sweating'
summary:
California's Death Valley is one of the hottest, driest places on Earth. In summer, temperatures there often climb above 49 degrees Celsius (120 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet one shrub, the Arizona honeysweet, does more than survive there. It thrives. Now scientists have learned one of its secrets: it cools itself by, basically, sweating.

Plants release water vapor through tiny pores called stomata on their leaves and stems. This process is called transpiration. Scientists say it works a lot like sweating.

Researchers at Michigan State University wanted to know how much this cooling helps the honeysweet survive. They collected seeds from 223 wild honeysweets in and near Death Valley. In the lab, they grew more than 1,200 seedlings at a comfortable 30 degrees C (86 degrees F). Then they slowly turned up the heat until it reached 60 degrees C (140 degrees F) for six to eight hours a day.

Some plants survived again and again. Some of their leaves stayed about 13 degrees C (23 degrees F) cooler than the air around them. When the scientists closed the leaves' pores to shut off the cooling, the plants did not live as long.

"This cooling makes the difference between life and death," says botanist Seung Yon Rhee.

Not all the plants survived, though. Some lasted only a few days, while others stayed healthy for weeks. Rhee suspects the difference may come from their DNA, much like how some people have brown eyes and others have blue.

The honeysweet already amazed scientists by growing fast in extreme heat. According to MSU plant biologist Karine Prado, it does photosynthesis best at 47 degrees C (117 degrees F), the highest peak-performance temperature for any plant. The team shared its new findings in August. They have not yet been reviewed by other scientists.
why_it_matters: Learning how a plant survives some of Earth's hottest conditions helps scientists understand the limits of life and how living things cope with extreme heat.

background_read: Plants make their own food through photosynthesis, using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
They take in gases and release water vapor through tiny pores in their leaves, and that escaping water helps cool them, much as sweat cools people.
Deserts like Death Valley get very little rain and extreme heat, so plants there need special ways to survive.
Scientists study such plants to learn how living things cope with very high temperatures.
